extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; general educated public interested in medicine, physiology, forensic questions, and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether death by hanging is painful, using physiological mechanisms, eyewitness and experimental reports, and comparative analysis with other forms of asphyxia; also includes a companion philosophical discussion on criteria for judging materialist theories. Targeted at informing lay and medically-interested readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of mechanism of death (broken neck vs asphyxia vs apoplexy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether death arose from cervical fracture, asphyxia, or a congestive apoplexy; the text states that a broken neck rarely occurs in executions and that death is usually due to asphyxia or apoplexy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clinical/observational evidence: in some heavy or aged persons a sudden shock may burst a blood-vessel producing immediate unconsciousness (apoplexy); otherwise death commonly follows asphyxia. The presence or absence of vertebral fracture, bleeding into brain-substance, and the pattern/timing of unconsciousness and respiratory failure help distinguish mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observable timing and signs of unconsciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate onset of insensibility from eyewitness timing and observable signs (motionlessness, small convulsive movements, quivering, 'sparks' before eyes, rattling or roaring in ears).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use objective timing (watch readings), look for immediate motionlessness, short interval to slight muscular movements, and sensory reports from survivors/performers. The author's eyewitness account: body motionless, slight drawings of feet at ~1m10s, then still — interpreted as painless death due to rapid unconsciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of eyewitness and experimental reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider testimonies of executed persons, rescuable suicides, performers who simulated hanging, and self-experimenters (e.g., Morgagni/Cesalpinus accounts, Harnshaw, Scott, Fleischmann, Devergie).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent, concordant reports across different observers and experimenters (reports of immediate stupor, loss of sensation, pleasurable feelings preceding unconsciousness, inability to move arms/legs or think) strengthen the conclusion that hanging is painless. Note exceptional cases (misplacement of rope leading to throat compression) and treat them separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological explanation: cerebral congestion from jugular compression
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain rapid unconsciousness physiologically: pressure on neck compresses jugular veins (which are lax) while carotid arteries continue pumping, producing rapid cerebral engorgement and insensibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mechanism is offered as the principal explanation for why unconsciousness precedes the later pangs of suffocation. The author notes a technical discussion is omitted, but emphasizes that cerebral congestion can render the victim unconscious within a minute, so the painful phase of asphyxia is not felt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of rope placement on respiration and sensations
rubrics_metrics.description: Different placements of the cord (between hyoid and chin vs over the larynx or compressing the throat) produce different physiological effects and timings of respiratory interference and sensations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-experiment descriptions (Fleischmann) show that a cord placed so as not to compress air-passages allows continued respiration for longer while causing venous congestion and warning symptoms (red face, dizziness, hissing in ears); compression of the larynx interferes with respiration sooner and produces symptoms more rapidly. Assess cases by rope placement to interpret sensations and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison criterion: insensibility precedes pangs of suffocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether a mode of death is 'painless' by whether unconsciousness is induced before the subjective pangs of asphyxia begin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this comparative standard to hanging and drowning: if secondary processes (cerebral congestion, apoplexy, concussion) render the person unconscious quickly, the later painful phase of suffocation is not experienced. Establish timing relationships from observations/experiments to support conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical/experimental caution: experiments on hanging are dangerous and unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that experiments on oneself to test sensations during strangulation/hanging are hazardous because unconsciousness is insidious and can prevent self-rescue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid or strictly control self-experimentation; the author notes multiple near-fatal attempts and warns that many who 'tried' out of curiosity were rescued or might have unintentionally died. Treat self-experiment reports with caution for safety and reliability reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation/correlation of forces as explanatory standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Require that scientific/philosophical accounts recognize that energy (force) is a persistent quantity which changes form but is not annihilated — 'the universe contains a fixed quantity' of energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the principle of conservation/correlation of forces as a standard for physical explanation: motion, heat, light, etc., are transformations of the same persisting energy. The essay treats this as a foundation against older views that regarded motion as merely a transient condition of matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish form versus substance and maintain clear conceptual distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Insist on distinguishing 'forms' (transient appearances) from 'substances' (the enduring bases) — matter, energy, and consciousness are presented as distinct substantive existences while their forms change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical and scientific clarity requires careful use of terms: confusing form (e.g., memory, motion) with substance leads to error. The essay argues that treating form as reality caused past mistakes (e.g., thinking fuel was annihilated because its form disappeared in combustion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'the inconceivability of the opposite' as a test of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Herbert Spencer's test — if the opposite is inconceivable, that supports the truth of a proposition (used here to argue consciousness cannot plausibly be produced solely by organization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ inconceivability as a heuristic for philosophical judgment: because one cannot conceive how modes of matter and motion could produce feeling, the author asserts consciousness has independent existence. Note this is a philosophical heuristic rather than empirical proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of philosophical coherence: premises must support permanent conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge philosophical systems by internal coherence — a system that denies a substantive ego but claims permanent, real conclusions is self-contradictory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid theories that undercut the very basis of knowledge they claim (e.g., declaring the perceiving consciousness unreal while asserting permanence of external matter). Logical consistency and non-self-undermining premises are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical criterion: account for observable body–mind interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any plausible theory must accommodate well-known empirical facts that bodily states affect mind (toothache, fever, injury) and mental states affect body (fright inducing disease or death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that philosophical or scientific accounts explain these interactions rather than dismissing them; the essay uses everyday examples (sleep arousal, effects of a blow on the head) to demand that theories of consciousness and matter explain the empirical interplay.
